summary: This memo describes how to use Adobe's Secure Real-Time Media Flow Protocol (RTMFP) to carry video, audio, and data messages for Adobe Flash communications. It covers cryptographic methods, data formats, and flow control. It is informational and documents a vendor protocol rather than an IETF standard.

plainLanguage.summary: Adobe Flash needed a way to send live video and chat between computers. This document explains the special delivery system Adobe made for that, written down so others can understand it.

questions: how does adobe flash send media
how does adobe flash send video
subtitle: How to send video, audio and data through RTMFP for Flash platform communication.

tldr.problem: Adobe Flash applications need a way to send real-time video, audio and data between computers, both between clients and servers and directly between peers, with encryption and integrity protection.
tldr.mechanism: RTMFP (Secure Real-Time Media Flow Protocol) is a general transport protocol, and this specification defines a cryptography profile and messaging format for Flash platform communications, including certificate handling, key agreement using Diffie-Hellman, AES-128 encryption, HMAC verification, and session keying.
tldr.outcome: Flash platform applications can use RTMFP to stream media with strong encryption and support for both client-server and peer-to-peer communication patterns. The specification has been implemented in Adobe Media Server and Flash Player.

today: RFC 7425 is an Informational specification of a vendor protocol. It documents how Adobe Flash platform applications use RTMFP for real-time media communication and is still the definition of the Flash RTMFP profile for implementations that need interoperability with Adobe systems or legacy Flash deployments. With the decline of Flash in web browsers, new applications are rare, but the specification remains relevant for existing Flash-based streaming systems, particularly in enterprise and media delivery contexts.

sections.title: Introduction
sections.content:
The Secure Real-Time Media Flow Protocol (RTMFP) is a general-purpose transport for real-time media and data over IP networks. This specification defines how the Flash platform, which includes Flash Player and Adobe Media Server, uses RTMFP to send video, audio, and data messages in both client-server (where computers talk to a central server) and peer-to-peer (where computers talk directly to each other) scenarios.

Flash platform communications traditionally used the Real-Time Messaging Protocol (RTMP) over TCP, but RTMFP offers advantages for real-time streaming over IP networks. This specification documents the concrete cryptography profile that Flash uses with RTMFP, replacing abstract security decisions with specific algorithms and formats.
sections.plainLanguage: RTMFP is a system for sending video and audio quickly over the Internet. This document explains how Adobe Flash uses it with special security so messages are scrambled and verified as real.

sections.title: Cryptography Profile
sections.content:
The cryptography profile defines how RTMFP sessions are secured. The specification uses Advanced Encryption Standard (AES) in CBC mode with 128-bit keys to encrypt data, HMAC-SHA256 for message authentication, and Diffie-Hellman (DH) key exchange for establishing shared secrets between endpoints.

Endpoints are identified by certificates that contain a DH public key and optional additional information such as a hostname. The fingerprint of the certificate (its SHA-256 hash) serves as a unique peer identifier. During session setup, endpoints exchange keying components containing ephemeral DH public keys or references to static keys. The protocol supports multiple Diffie-Hellman groups (1024-bit group 2 required; 1536-bit group 5 and 2048-bit group 14 recommended). Sessions use an initialization vector (IV) of all zeros for CBC mode encryption.

The specification defines a default session key for initial communication before session-specific keys are negotiated. Default keys are used during the handshake, after which endpoints compute session-specific encryption, HMAC, and nonce keys using HMAC-based key derivation from the DH shared secret.
sections.plainLanguage: To keep messages secret, Flash computers use a math trick called Diffie-Hellman so they can agree on a secret number even if someone is listening. Then they use that secret to scramble messages with AES, which is a very strong lock, and add a checksum to prove the message was not changed.

sections.title: Certificates and Endpoint Identification
sections.content:
Endpoints are identified by certificates encoded as sequences of RTMFP options. A certificate's fingerprint (the SHA-256 hash of the canonical section) is the peer ID. Certificates can contain a static Diffie-Hellman public key for use across multiple sessions, or indicate support for ephemeral (temporary) keys that differ for each session.

The specification defines several certificate options: a hostname for server identification; an 'Accepts Ancillary Data' flag; a static DH public key and the group it belongs to; ephemeral DH group support; and extra randomness bytes. Clients connect to servers using an Endpoint Discriminator (EPD) that identifies the server by its fingerprint, hostname, or server URI (the rtmfp:// URL). This profile does not use a public key infrastructure; any properly encoded certificate is considered authentic, and identity is implied by successful encrypted communication with the holder of the corresponding private key.

The specification includes a glare resolution mechanism (used when two endpoints initiate sessions to each other concurrently) based on lexicographic comparison of certificates.
sections.plainLanguage: Each computer has a certificate that is like its ID card. It contains a public key that others use to check messages and a fingerprint that proves who you are. The server's address is sent in a special URI format like rtmfp://server.example.com/app.

sections.title: RTMP Messages and Flows
sections.content:
RTMFP flows are unidirectional and carry RTMP messages. Each flow has metadata indicating the RTMP stream ID and a receive intent (whether the receiver wants messages in original order or as they arrive). Messages carried on flows have a message type (8 bits), timestamp (32 bits), and payload. The protocol maps RTMP message types used by the Flash platform (such as audio data, video data, and control messages) onto RTMFP flows.

To maintain RTMP ordering semantics across multiple unordered flows, the specification defines Flow Synchronization messages (RTMP User Control Event type 34) that act as barriers, telling receivers to wait until the same barrier has arrived on multiple flows before delivering further messages.

The client-server connection establishes a main control flow on stream ID 0 for NetConnection messages, and additional flows for media streams. The client sends a 'connect' command to the server and must send a 'setPeerInfo' command listing its candidate addresses (to help the server determine if the client is behind a Network Address Translator). The server responds with result or error and may send a 'Set Keepalive Timers' control message to advise keepalive periods for the server connection and peer-to-peer connections.
sections.plainLanguage: Messages come on separate channels called flows, each carrying one type of data like video or audio. The protocol numbers the flows and marks them with timestamps. For video conference between a client and server, there is a main control channel and separate channels for the video, audio, and other data.

sections.title: Peer-to-Peer Streaming
sections.content:
Two Flash clients can stream directly to each other using the peer-to-peer model. To subscribe to a stream from a peer, a subscriber client learns the peer's ID (fingerprint) through application-specific means and creates a new flow to that peer, sending an RTMP 'play' command. The publisher, on accepting the control flow and command, opens return flows for the stream media associated with the subscriber's control flow.

The server acts as an Introducer, using forward and redirect messages to help the subscriber and publisher establish an RTMFP session if they do not already have one. The specification supports closing the connection when either side closes or rejects the control flow, or by terminating the underlying RTMFP session.
sections.plainLanguage: Two people can watch a video directly from each other without a server in the middle. One person asks the other to share their video, and they make a direct connection. If they do not know how to find each other, a server helps them connect.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
This profile does not use a public key infrastructure. Client endpoints SHOULD use static DH keys in their certificates to prevent man-in-the-middle attacks against specific client identities. Each new client-server connection MUST use a new certificate with a distinct fingerprint. Servers MAY use ephemeral DH keys for forward secrecy, since clients connect to servers by URI rather than by peer ID, making server peer ID forgery irrelevant.

Without session sequence numbers, replayed encrypted packets could appear as new flows. Session sequence numbers (which the specification supports optionally) detect and reject duplicates and replays. CBC mode with a null IV can reveal when two packets contain identical plaintext; however, the flow sequence number ensures the first cipher block is usually unique. Packet verification uses HMAC-SHA256 when negotiated, or a simple 16-bit ones' complement checksum inside the encrypted packet when not. When HMAC is absent, the checksum provides essentially cryptographic 16-bit protection.
sections.plainLanguage: Every message gets checked with math so you know it was not changed on the way. To prevent someone pretending to be someone else, the computers check that messages can be encrypted and decrypted correctly with each other's keys. Repeat attacks (playing the same message twice) can be stopped by numbering messages.
